How to Make Dried Flowers from Cotton: A Simple DIY Guide for Stunning Home Decor Dried flowers are a timeless way to add natural beauty to your home, and cotton flowers are a unique choice for creating elegant, long-lasting arrangements. With their soft, fluffy texture and neutral tones, dried cotton flowers bring a rustic yet sophisticated charm to any space. Here’s a step-by-step guide to making your own dried cotton flowers. Materials You’ll Need: Fresh cotton stems (with bolls intact) Scissors or pruning shears Twine or rubber bands A dark, dry, and well-ventilated area Step 1: Harvest the Cotton Stems If you’re growing cotton, wait until the bolls are fully open and fluffy. Carefully cut the stems at an angle, leaving enough length for arranging. If you’re purchasing cotton stems, ensure they’re fresh and free from damage. Step 2: Prepare for Drying Remove any excess leaves or debris from the stems. Group 3-5 stems together and secure them with twine or rubber bands. Avoid overcrowding to ensure proper airflow during the drying process. Step 3: Hang to Dry Find a dark, dry, and well-ventilated space, such as a closet or attic. Hang the cotton stems upside down to preserve their shape. Avoid direct sunlight, as it can cause the cotton to yellow or become brittle. Step 4: Wait Patiently Allow the cotton stems to dry for 2-3 weeks. Check periodically to ensure they’re drying evenly and there’s no mold or moisture buildup. Step 5: Style and Display Once fully dried, your cotton flowers are ready to use! Arrange them in vases, create wreaths, or incorporate them into floral arrangements. Their neutral color pairs beautifully with other dried flowers, greenery, or seasonal decor. Dried cotton flowers are not only easy to make but also incredibly versatile. Whether you’re decorating your home or creating a thoughtful gift, this DIY project is a wonderful way to bring a touch of nature indoors. Try it today and enjoy the timeless beauty of dried cotton flowers! Share your creations on LinkedIn and inspire others to try this simple yet stunning DIY project!

Did you know? The strawberry isn’t actually a fruit, but a flower 🍓
 
 We all call it a fruit, but botany disagrees. What you eat is the swollen receptacle of the strawberry flower. The real fruits are those tiny yellowish dots on the surface.
 
 Each dot is called an achene. Each achene is a true fruit containing one seed. So one strawberry is actually hundreds of tiny fruits attached to modified flower tissue.
 
 In most fruits like apples or peaches, the flesh grows from the ovary. Strawberries flip that. The red, juicy part evolved to attract animals and spread seeds. 
 
 A small detail that completely changes how we see something ordinary. Nature doesn’t follow our labels. It follows its own rules.
 
 Follow @explain_hub_01 for more
